cards.front: In chemistry, what is a pure substance?
cards.back: A **pure substance** contains only one element or one compound. Everyday 'pure' (natural or safe) does not mean this.
cards.hint: Count how many different kinds of particle are present.

cards.front: How does the melting behaviour of a pure substance differ from that of a mixture?
cards.back: A pure substance melts at a **characteristic temperature** at a given pressure. A mixture usually melts over a **range of temperatures**.

cards.front: Why do dissolved substances end up in different places on chromatography paper?
cards.back: Each substance has a different balance of **attraction to the solvent and to the paper**, so each travels a different distance.
cards.hint: Think about what the solvent is pulling against as it rises.

cards.back: A **formulation** is a mixture whose components are present in carefully measured amounts to give a useful product.

cards.front: Why can changing the proportions in a formulation change its properties?
cards.back: The **amounts of each component** control the result, so the same ingredients in different proportions can behave differently.
cards.hint: Compare a product made with more of one ingredient to one made with less.

cards.front: What are the steps to run paper chromatography?
cards.back: 1) Put a sample spot on a **pencil baseline** near the bottom of the paper. 2) Stand the paper in solvent, keeping the baseline above the solvent level. 3) Mark the **solvent front** before the paper dries.

cards.front: Why must the baseline on chromatography paper be drawn in pencil rather than ink?
cards.back: Ink could **dissolve in the solvent** and produce extra spots, which would confuse the result.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the marks when the solvent reaches them.

cards.back: The **solvent front** is the furthest point the solvent reaches on the chromatography paper. It is marked before the paper dries.

cards.front: What is the equation for an Rf value, and what are its units?
cards.back: $R_f=\frac{\text{distance travelled by spot}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent front}}$. Both distances are measured from the **baseline**, and the Rf value has **no unit**.

cards.front: A spot travels 3 cm from the baseline and the solvent front travels 6 cm. What is the Rf value?
cards.back: $R_f=\frac{3\,\mathrm{cm}}{6\,\mathrm{cm}}=0.5$. The Rf value has no unit.
cards.hint: Divide the spot's distance by the solvent front's distance.

cards.front: What does a chromatogram with several spots tell you about the sample?
cards.back: One spot suggests one dissolved substance. **Several spots** show the sample is a mixture.

cards.front: Why is matching the height of two spots not enough to prove they are the same substance?
cards.back: Spots at the same height **may** be the same substance, but different substances can travel the same distance, so matching positions do not prove identity.
cards.hint: Consider what determines how far a spot travels.

cards.front: Why must Rf values only be compared when obtained under the same conditions?
cards.back: Rf values **depend on the solvent and conditions**, so results from different conditions cannot be fairly compared.

cards.front: Why might a substance in a sample not show up as a spot on a chromatogram?
cards.back: If it is **insoluble in the chosen solvent**, it will not travel up the paper, so it leaves no spot.
cards.hint: Think about whether the substance can dissolve in the solvent used.
